title: Aqueous eutectic hydrogel electrolytes enable flexible thermocells with a wide operating temperature range

segments.text: Thermocells (TECs) can directly convert thermal energy into electricity via the thermogalvanic effect of redox ions.
The employment of hydrogel electrolytes allows for the facile fabrication of flexible quasi-solid-state TECs with low health hazard, easy scalability and eco-friendliness.

In contrast, conventional hydrogel electrolytes cannot adapt to a sufficiently wide working temperature range, as they inevitably freeze under sub-zero temperatures and dry out under elevated temperatures, resulting in loss in both mechanical flexibility and ion transport capability.

Herein, a hydrogel electrolyte using low-concentration redox ions with excellent freeze-tolerance and self-humidifying capabilities is rationally designed by regulating the hydration effect, affording a flexible quasi-solid-state aqueous TEC system that can continually work under a wide temperature range (-15 degrees C to 70 degrees C).
It also demonstrates long-term environmental stability without the need for encapsulation or packaging.

The colligative properties of the hydrogel electrolyte can suppress ice crystallization, and in-depth molecular dynamics simulations reveal that a vital underlying mechanism is the strong coordination effect of Li+ ions with water molecules over a wide range of temperatures.

The TEC designed in this work shows high adaptability to temperature fluctuations and environmental changes, and offers a promising route to promote low-grade heat harvesting under extreme environmental conditions.

title: Multiple redox system for energy harvesting from ubiquitous temperature fluctuations

segments.text: Thermogalvanic cells, which convert heat to electricity, typically require complex thermal and electrical designs to maintain a sufficient spatial temperature difference with low electrical impedance, thereby limiting their practical applications.
Herein, we present a multiple redox system (MRS) designed to harvest energy from ubiquitous temporal temperature fluctuations rather than fixed thermal gradients.
The MRS employs two thermogalvanic half cells containing an electrolyte composed of a redox pair with reaction entropies of opposite signs, separated by a cation-selective membrane.

Cyclic voltammetry and open-circuit voltage measurements demonstrated the fundamental principle of this device, confirming that the electromotive force generated (with a temperature coefficient of similar to 1.2 mV K-1) was consistent with the difference in the temperature-dependent redox potential of each half cell (similar to 1.4 mV K-1), with the base temperature located near room temperature.

Loading experiments revealed the repeated generation of an alternating current power under cyclic temperature modulations above and below a central base temperature at which the redox potentials of the half cells were identical.

Enhanced energy conversion efficiency, with a cumulative energy output of 3.9 mJ from a total temperature-change history of 60 K, was achieved by reducing the electrode gap and modularizing several MRS devices.
As a proof-of-concept, the MRS was successfully used to convert ambient air-temperature changes into sufficient electrical energy and activate a direct current (DC)-to-DC converter.

Our device-engineering investigations highlight the potential applicability of the MRS beyond a single thermogalvanic cell, with downscaling of the device size leading to marked improvements in power and response speed by suppressing the impedance and heat capacity.
This study contributes to the realization of clean, ubiquitous, and self-sustaining power supply systems utilizing ambient thermal energy.
